classification.difficultyReason: Direct evaluation by recognising whole-number and fractional powers of the logarithm base.

questions.mappingNote: Every assigned part asks for direct logarithm evaluation; parts j–l extend the fractional-power evaluations demonstrated in Example 1(c–d).
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a logarithm as an exponent. Rewrite the argument as a power of its base, as demonstrated in Example 1, including fractional powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct evaluation by recognising whole-number and fractional powers of the logarithm base.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms of reciprocals, including fractional negative powers, using the logarithm definition.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a)–(i) apply the definition to reciprocal integer powers. Parts (j)–(l) apply Example 2's common-base method to reciprocal arguments. Evaluation is the directly assessed skill; negative and fractional indices support the method.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines a logarithm as an exponent. Example 1 rewrites arguments as powers of the logarithmic base; Example 2 on page 2 converts to an exponential equation and equates exponents after rewriting both sides with a common base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms of reciprocals, including fractional negative powers, using the logarithm definition.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert between logarithmic and exponential equations, isolating the logarithm or exponent where necessary.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e isolate the logarithm and convert to exponential form. Parts f–i convert an exponential equation to logarithmic form and isolate x. Part j first isolates the exponential term.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines logarithms by equivalence with exponential form. Page 2 Example 3 isolates an argument or exponent and converts between these forms, retaining exact logarithmic answers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert between logarithmic and exponential equations, isolating the logarithm or exponent where necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms by constructing exponential equations and expressing both sides with a common base, including fractional powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, c and d use a common numerical base. Parts b, e and f express square roots as fractional powers before equating exponents. Every part follows the explicitly requested exponential-equation method.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines logarithmic and exponential equivalence. Page 2 Example 2 sets a logarithm equal to a, converts to an exponential equation, rewrites both sides with a common base and equates exponents, including square roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate logarithms by constructing exponential equations and expressing both sides with a common base, including fractional powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Nested logarithms and logarithmic exponents require successive conversions between logarithmic and exponential form.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 is in the continuation of Section A above the 22B band. Parts a and b apply the definition twice; c and d convert logarithmic equations to exponential form; e and f combine common-base exponent comparison with that definition. Example 3 supports leaving d as an exact logarithm.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a logarithm to convert to exponential form. For logarithmic exponents, rewrite numerical bases as powers of a common base and equate indices, as in Example 2. Convert the remaining logarithmic equation back to exponential form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Nested logarithms and logarithmic exponents require successive conversions between logarithmic and exponential form.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires generalising three evaluations and proving the power law from the logarithm definition and index laws.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 precedes the 22B topic band and belongs to 22A. Parts (a)–(c) establish the pattern; part (d) directly assesses deduction and proof of the logarithmic power law. The answer-book proof in Section B 8(b), PDF page 48, corroborates this method.
questions.methodNote: Use the logarithm definition to convert each given into exponential form, apply the power-of-a-power index law, then convert back. Prove the conjecture with a general exponent, following the same sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires generalising three evaluations and proving the power law from the logarithm definition and index laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluates two products using exponential form, then requires a general conjecture and proof.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 belongs to the continuing 22A exercise above the 22B band. Its final part directly assesses deducing and proving the product law, making laws-of-logarithms the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Convert logarithmic statements into exponential form, multiply powers with the same base, and translate back. The product-law proof on page 4 uses arbitrary logarithms m and n.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluates two products using exponential form, then requires a general conjecture and proof.

classification.difficultyReason: Generalise two quotient evaluations and prove the resulting logarithm law using exponential form.

questions.mappingNote: The source places question 8 before the 22B heading, making it a continuation of 22A. Its culminating conjecture and proof directly assess the laws-of-logarithms skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a logarithm to express the givens as powers, apply the quotient index law, and convert back. The theorem proof on page 4 models deriving logarithm laws from exponential form; pages 5–6 confirm the quotient law.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise two quotient evaluations and prove the resulting logarithm law using exponential form.

classification.difficultyReason: Relates logarithms with different product bases and proves a general identity using exponential form.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 precedes the 22B topic band and continues Exercise 22A. Its different product bases and general proof most closely assess evaluation and simplification of logarithmic expressions.
questions.methodNote: Use the logarithm definition to convert each given to exponential form, combine powers with a common base, and convert the result back to logarithmic form. Page 2 models exponential conversion; page 4 provides the nearby product-law proof.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Relates logarithms with different product bases and proves a general identity using exponential form.

classification.difficultyReason: Bound each logarithm between consecutive integers by comparing the argument with consecutive powers, without a calculator.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 precedes the 22B topic band and belongs to 22A, confirmed by the individual Section A answer entries. Defining a logarithm is the closest catalogue skill because these parts assess exponent bounds rather than logarithm laws.
questions.methodNote: The logarithm is the exponent producing the argument. Compare the argument with consecutive integer powers of its base; all five bases exceed 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Bound each logarithm between consecutive integers by comparing the argument with consecutive powers, without a calculator.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain why base 1 fails to define a unique logarithm using the exponential definition.

questions.mappingNote: The question tests the restriction that a logarithmic base must differ from 1, stated in the definition on page 1; page 2 demonstrates conversion to exponential form.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a logarithm as an exponent, converting a logarithmic statement into its exponential form.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain why base 1 fails to define a unique logarithm using the exponential definition.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine product, quotient and power laws, including fractional coefficients and ratios of logarithms.
